import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 699

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/699](https://www.erdosproblems.com/699)
-/

namespace Erdos699

/-- Sylvester and Schur: for $1 \le i \le n/2$ there is a prime $p > i$ dividing `n.choose i`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/AllenGrahamHart/FormalConjectures-Bench/blob/482dacc4d9335240f26218cdc62032da3100392b/formalizations/erdos699/Erdos699Formalization.lean#L7679"]
theorem sylvester_schur (n i : ℕ) (hi : 1 ≤ i) (hi_half : i ≤ n / 2) :
    ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.choose n i := by
  sorry

/--
**Erdős Problem 699.** Is it true that for every $1 \le i < j \le n / 2$ there exists a prime
$p \ge i$ with $p \mid \gcd\big(\binom{n}{i}, \binom{n}{j}\big)$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_699 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ n i j : ℕ,
      1 ≤ i →
      i < j →
      j ≤ n / 2 →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i ≤ p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j) := by
  sorry

/-- Erdős and Szekeres conjectured that, apart from a finite exceptional set of triples `(n, i, j)`,
one can always take `p > i` in the prime divisor statement. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_szekeres_strengthening : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ), ∀ n i j : ℕ,
      1 ≤ i →
      i < j →
      j ≤ n / 2 →
      (n, i, j) ∉ E →
      ∃ p : ℕ, p.Prime ∧ i < p ∧ p ∣ Nat.gcd (Nat.choose n i) (Nat.choose n j) := by
  sorry

end Erdos699

findings.description: The single `∃ E : Finset (ℕ × ℕ × ℕ)` before `∀ n i j` asserts globally finitely many exceptions to the strict bound `i < p`, including finitely many exceptions with i = 2 and with i = 3. This is a substantive interpretation of the source's less precise phrase 'except in a few special cases'. The primary paper discusses parametrized low-index exceptional cases separately and specifically describes 'a few incidental counterexamples' for i ≥ 4. It does not explicitly assert that the low-index cases contribute only finitely many triples. Consequently, global finiteness deserves clarification rather than being attributed unconditionally to Erdős and Szekeres. This is an ambiguity, not a demonstrated disproof: I have not established infinitely many exceptional triples.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős–Szekeres, 'Some number theoretic problems on binomial coefficients' (1978), pp. 97–98, equation (5) and the following discussion, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-46.pdf: the strict inequality 'holds except in a few special cases'; the authors then discuss i = 2 with n = 2^r and factorizations of 2^r − 1, and i = 3 with numbers 3^r + 1, before saying 'For i ≥ 4 there should only be a few incidental counterexamples to (5).' https://www.erdosproblems.com/699 preserves this distinction and does not explicitly state global finiteness.
findings.suggested_fix: Seek a reference explicitly supporting finiteness over all triples before retaining the present attribution. A conservative finite-exception variant supported by the paper's more specific discussion would use `4 ≤ i` instead of `1 ≤ i`, with a matching docstring, and discuss the i = 2,3 exceptional cases separately. Do not assume that finitely many exceptional cases or families necessarily means finitely many triples.

reformulations.difference: Conjecture 1 in the original paper bounds the greatest prime factor of the gcd below by i; Lean instead asks for some prime divisor of that gcd which is at least i.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For the admissible indices both binomial coefficients and their gcd are positive. With i ≥ 1, `i ≤ g.primeFactors.sup id` is equivalent to the existence of a prime p ≥ i dividing g: a maximum satisfying the bound supplies a witness, and any witness is bounded by the maximum. The empty prime-factor set gives 0 and cannot satisfy the positive threshold. This pointwise equivalence and the full universally quantified equivalence were proved independently in /workspace/review/max_prime_equivalence.lean.

could_not_verify: Erdos699.erdos_szekeres_strengthening: the cited qualitative wording does not settle whether global finiteness, including the low-index exceptional cases, was intended. This unresolved source interpretation is the questionable finding above.
review.notes: Checked all three declarations, their quantifier scopes, answer semantics and boundary cases. Natural floor division matches the ordinary half-bound, and the hypotheses exclude zero binomial coefficients and zero gcds. Lean evaluations through n = 100 found no main-statement or Sylvester–Schur counterexamples; the four strict exceptions were (10,3,5), (16,2,6), (28,3,14), and (28,5,14). Independently proved that the strengthening's Finset formulation means finiteness of the entire bad-triple set, equivalently validity for all sufficiently large n. The external Sylvester–Schur declaration exactly matches the file. Its proof passed a kernel check after scratch-only compatibility repairs to one derivative helper and four elementary arithmetic proofs; its axioms were only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. All review artifacts and compatibility edits were confined to /workspace/review; the target file is unchanged.
